Nonetheless, the complex deposition process and susceptibility to environmental and mechanical degradation remain a critical drawback. In the next section, inorganic multilayer systems are introduced as a solution that emerged to address some of these issues, particularly the flexibility of TCGDB systems. Furthermore, a 100nm TMT structure demonstrates lower sheet resistance (5 Ω/sq.) compared to a thicker TCO film (200nm: 15 Ω/sq.), and upholds comparable optical transparencies. In terms of barrier properties, the TMT relies predominantly on the TCO microstructure, however, slight improvements were observed from the insertion of an ultra-thin metal interlayer (Table 2). For example, WVTR in the range of 10-4 g/m2/day was achieved with a sputtered IZO/Ag/IZO structure,48 compared to the 10-2 g/m2/day with a single IZO layer (Table 1). Nevertheless, monolithically integrated inorganic multilayers tend to replicate defects from the under-film in subsequent depositions. Hence, the process is unforgiving, and the location and spatial density of defects do not change for samples with particle contaminations or abrupt changes in surface morphology. Consequently, compromised samples yield little to no improvement in WVTR. Thus, a surface planarizing layer (i.e., polymer) is required to take full advantage of the multilayer barrier structure. Unfortunately, polymers are an electrically insulating component that remains largely unexplored for use in TCGDBs. 7/52 DE-EE0010241 Nicolas Gaillard Figure 4: Concept image of a TMT multilayer structure on a polymer substrate.
